quote: For antipsychotic **rechallenge**: wait **at least 2 weeks** after full resolution, choose a **lower-potency or atypical agent** at a low starting dose, titrate slowly, and monitor temperature, CK, and autonomic signs; recurrence can occur at any point after resolution, so shared decision-making and close follow-up are essential [5].
problem: The rechallenge guidance omits the standard prohibition on long-acting injectable/depot antipsychotics after NMS. This stem is a group-home patient with schizoaffective disorder and implied adherence concerns, and this same volume's mania case pushes 'LAI consideration in poor adherence' — so the resident's instinct here is a depot, and 'atypical agent at a low starting dose' superficially permits paliperidone or aripiprazole LAI. If NMS recurs, a depot cannot be withdrawn; the exposure continues for weeks while the syndrome runs its course, which is the mechanism by which depot-associated NMS is more prolonged and more lethal.
replacement: For antipsychotic **rechallenge**: wait **at least 2 weeks** after full resolution (longer if the offending agent was a depot), correct dehydration, electrolyte derangement, and iron deficiency first, then choose a **lower-potency or atypical oral agent** — **never a long-acting injectable, which cannot be withdrawn if NMS recurs** — at a low starting dose, titrate slowly, and monitor temperature, CK, and autonomic signs; recurrence can occur at any point after resolution, so shared decision-making and close follow-up are essential [5].
basis: Standard NMS rechallenge guidance (Caroff & Mann and Strawn/Keck/Caroff NMS reviews; Pileggi & Cook, Ann Pharmacother 2016 — this page's own reference [5]): minimum two-week interval after complete resolution, lowest-potency effective agent, slow titration, correction of dehydration and iron deficiency, avoidance of the original agent, and explicit avoidance of depot preparations.

quote: A 2025 systematic review/meta-analysis supports **efficacy against depressive symptoms and, in the acute setting, suicidality**, with dissociation, sedation, and transient blood-pressure elevation as the main tolerability issues and REMS-mandated monitoring [8].
problem: This teaches residents that esketamine has demonstrated efficacy against suicidality itself. The pivotal trials behind the MDSI indication (ASPIRE I and II) separated from placebo on MADRS depressive symptoms at 24 hours but did not reach significance on the suicidality-severity endpoint (CGI-SS-r), and the US label carries an explicit limitation that effectiveness in preventing suicide or reducing suicidal ideation has not been demonstrated. A resident who believes the drug treats suicidality may let it substitute for the observation intensity, means-safety work, and disposition an acutely suicidal patient actually needs — and this page reaches for esketamine specifically 'given emerging TRD status and passive SI.'
replacement: A 2025 systematic review/meta-analysis supports **efficacy against depressive symptoms**, including rapid symptom reduction in patients presenting with acute suicidal ideation, with dissociation, sedation, and transient blood-pressure elevation as the main tolerability issues and REMS-mandated monitoring [8]. State the limit explicitly: the MDSI indication rests on rapid improvement in *depressive symptoms*, not on a demonstrated effect on suicidality — the pivotal ASPIRE trials did not separate from placebo on the suicidality-severity endpoint, and the label states that effectiveness in preventing suicide or reducing suicidal ideation has not been demonstrated. Esketamine does not reduce the need for monitoring, means restriction, or safety planning.
basis: Spravato (esketamine) US prescribing information, Limitations of Use; Fu et al., J Clin Psychiatry 2020 (ASPIRE I) and Ionescu et al., Int J Neuropsychopharmacol 2021 (ASPIRE II), in which the key secondary CGI-SS-r endpoint at 24 hours was not statistically significant. Settled by reading how suicidality is pooled and reported in Fountoulakis 2025 [8] alongside the label's Limitations of Use.

quote: **pregnancy status is decisive** — both lithium (Ebstein anomaly risk, though lower than historically cited) and especially **valproate (neural-tube defects, ~9–11% major malformation and dose-dependent neurodevelopmental harm)** are avoided when pregnancy is possible.
problem: The sentence places lithium in the same avoidance tier as valproate while conceding in its own parenthesis that the Ebstein risk is lower than historically cited — it draws the historical conclusion from the corrected number. Lithium is not withheld from patients who could become pregnant: absolute first-trimester Ebstein risk is roughly 1 in 1,000–2,000, and the relapse risk of stopping a mood stabiliser peripartum is an order of magnitude larger. A resident applying this rule will deny the one agent with an anti-suicidal signal to a large share of the women they treat, or stop it abruptly on a positive pregnancy test, which is the highest-risk move available.
replacement: **pregnancy status is decisive** — **valproate (neural-tube defects, ~9–11% major malformation and dose-dependent neurodevelopmental harm) is avoided in anyone who could become pregnant** unless a pregnancy-prevention programme is in place; **lithium is not in that tier** — the absolute Ebstein risk is far lower than historically cited (on the order of 1 in 1,000–2,000), so lithium is used with contraception and preconception counselling, level monitoring across the trimesters, and fetal echocardiography where indicated, and is rarely stopped abruptly given the high peripartum relapse risk.
basis: CANMAT/ISBD 2018 (this page's reference [1]) and ACOG guidance on bipolar disorder in pregnancy; Patorno et al., NEJM 2017 (lithium and first-trimester cardiac malformations); MHRA/FDA valproate pregnancy-prevention requirements. Valproate and lithium do not share a risk tier and should not be taught as if they do.

quote: **Immediate management:** **stop all dopamine antagonists** (including metoclopramide); ICU-level supportive care — IV fluids, active cooling, correct electrolytes, protect renal function against rhabdomyolysis.
problem: The immediate-management list for a stuporous, rigid, febrile, volume-depleted, immobile patient omits venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. Pulmonary embolism is a recognised leading cause of death in NMS and malignant catatonia, driven by exactly this combination of prolonged immobility, rigidity, and dehydration. A resident who works this checklist will stop the antipsychotic, hydrate, cool, and monitor renal function — and still miss the complication most likely to kill the patient while everything else is going right.
replacement: **Immediate management:** **stop all dopamine antagonists** (including metoclopramide); ICU-level supportive care — IV fluids, active cooling, correct electrolytes, protect renal function against rhabdomyolysis, and start **VTE prophylaxis** (pharmacologic unless contraindicated, plus mechanical) given prolonged immobility and rigidity; attend to aspiration risk and skin/pressure care for the same reason.
basis: NMS and malignant catatonia reviews consistently list pulmonary embolism among the leading causes of death, attributed to immobility, rigidity and volume depletion (Pileggi & Cook 2016 and Ware et al. 2018, this page's references [4] and [5]); standard inpatient/ICU VTE-prophylaxis practice for immobilised patients.

quote: metabolic baseline (weight, BMI, lipids, HbA1c) before an atypical antipsychotic; ECG if considering agents with QT liability; pregnancy planning discussion; consider genotype only if it will change dosing decisions.
problem: The pre-prescribing checklist is complete for the atypical-antipsychotic option and empty for lithium, which the very next paragraph offers as a co-equal first choice for augmentation. Nothing tells the resident to obtain baseline creatinine/eGFR, TSH and calcium, or to draw a 12-hour trough level roughly five days after initiation and after every dose change — and nothing connects this patient's migraine history to the NSAID interaction that is the commonest outpatient route to lithium toxicity. The asymmetry teaches that lithium is the lower-effort option, which is the opposite of true; a resident following this list starts lithium blind and monitors it by symptom.
replacement: metabolic baseline (weight, BMI, lipids, HbA1c) before an atypical antipsychotic; **before lithium: creatinine/eGFR, TSH, calcium, urine pregnancy test, and a plan for a 12-hour trough level ~5 days after initiation and after every dose change, with counselling that NSAIDs (directly relevant to her migraines), thiazides, and ACE inhibitors/ARBs raise lithium levels**; ECG if considering agents with QT liability; pregnancy planning discussion; consider genotype only if it will change dosing decisions.
basis: APA and CANMAT lithium-initiation standards (baseline renal, thyroid and calcium studies; trough level approximately five days after initiation or any dose change). Note the interaction set is stated correctly elsewhere in this same volume — the mania case's 'NSAIDs/thiazides/ACE-I raise lithium' — but is absent from the one case that actually recommends starting lithium.

quote: A real-world cohort showed **guideline-concordant first-line regimens cut 30-day rehospitalization (OR 0.21) and any readmission (OR 0.39)** vs. no treatment [4]
problem: The comparator is stated as 'no treatment,' which does not match what the cited study is asking. A paper titled 'Does the Ranking Matter?' is set up to contrast first-line against lower-ranked or non-recommended regimens, not treatment against nothing — and 'no treatment' is a near-empty comparator group in an acute-mania admission cohort. If the true reference group is non-first-line pharmacotherapy, these odds ratios are a genuinely strong argument for guideline concordance; if it really is untreated patients, they are close to uninformative and should not be handed to residents as 'a compelling lever for shared decision-making,' because the first patient who pushes back will find the confound immediately.
replacement: A real-world cohort showed **guideline-concordant first-line regimens cut 30-day rehospitalization (OR 0.21) and any readmission (OR 0.39)** compared with patients not discharged on a CANMAT first-line regimen [4]
basis: Gomes et al., 'Does the Ranking Matter?', Can J Psychiatry 2023;68(8):605–612 — this page's reference [4]. Settled by reading the study's stated reference group in its methods and confirming which contrast produced OR 0.21 and OR 0.39; the replacement text above assumes the first-line vs non-first-line contrast and should be adjusted if the paper genuinely used an untreated comparator.

quote: Intranasal **esketamine** is FDA-approved as adjunct for TRD and for MDD with acute suicidal ideation/behavior.
problem: Esketamine's US treatment-resistant-depression indication was broadened to monotherapy in January 2025; it is no longer adjunct-only. On a page whose whole subject is sequencing, a resident taught this will conclude that a patient who cannot tolerate or will not continue an oral antidepressant is ineligible for esketamine and will not offer it. The distinction is also worth teaching in its own right, because the MDSI indication does still require concomitant oral antidepressant therapy — the two indications now differ.
replacement: Intranasal **esketamine** is FDA-approved for TRD — since January 2025 as **monotherapy** as well as adjunctively with an oral antidepressant — and, **in conjunction with an oral antidepressant**, for depressive symptoms in adults with MDD with acute suicidal ideation or behavior.
basis: FDA approval of Spravato as a standalone/monotherapy treatment for treatment-resistant depression in adults, January 2025; the MDSI indication remains worded 'in conjunction with an oral antidepressant.' Settled by the current Spravato prescribing information, section 1 (Indications and Usage).

quote: *anticholinergic* → supportive, remove agent, benzodiazepine ± physostigmine in select cases
problem: The one-screen summary compresses 'anticholinergic → benzodiazepine' with nothing marking that this applies to a frank anticholinergic toxidrome (the page's differential #3) rather than to the multifactorial delirium the page itself ranks first — 'UTI + anticholinergic (oxybutynin) + baseline cognitive vulnerability.' Read against this patient, the line licenses lorazepam, which is precisely the order the facilitator notes spend a paragraph calling 'the higher-stakes error,' and it sits two clauses from 'avoid reflexive haloperidol+lorazepam combos' in the same bullet. A resident scanning the summary at the bedside gives the benzodiazepine to a 74-year-old with hyperactive delirium and deepens it.
replacement: *anticholinergic toxidrome as the primary driver* → supportive, remove agent, benzodiazepine ± physostigmine in select cases — **this is the frank toxidrome only; where anticholinergic burden is one contributor to multifactorial delirium, as here, stop the offending drug but still avoid benzodiazepines**
basis: Internal contradiction with this page's own teaching point 2 and with its ranked differential, which correctly separates #1 (multifactorial delirium with anticholinergic contribution) from #3 (anticholinergic toxidrome as primary driver). Standard delirium guidance restricts benzodiazepines to withdrawal states and to anticholinergic/sympathomimetic toxidromes, not to delirium that merely has an anticholinergic contributor.

quote: NMS typically resolves over **days to ~2 weeks** with agent withdrawal and supportive care — slower than SS, which usually clears in 24–72 h [1][4][5].
problem: 'Clears in 24–72 h' holds for short-half-life serotonergic agents and is false for the one this patient is actually taking. Fluoxetine's active metabolite norfluoxetine has a half-life of days to weeks, so fluoxetine-associated serotonin toxicity can be both delayed in onset and prolonged well past 72 hours — which also weakens the tempo argument the case uses to exclude SS. A resident could stop fluoxetine, expect resolution by day three, read persisting abnormality as evidence for a competing diagnosis, or clear the patient for a subsequent serotonergic agent or an MAOI far too early.
replacement: NMS typically resolves over **days to ~2 weeks** with agent withdrawal and supportive care — usually slower than serotonin toxicity, which clears within 24–72 h **for short-half-life agents. With fluoxetine (norfluoxetine half-life of days to weeks) or an MAOI, both onset and resolution can be substantially delayed, and a 5-week washout is required before starting an MAOI** [1][4][5].
basis: Fluoxetine elimination half-life 1–4 days and norfluoxetine 4–16 days (US prescribing information), hence the standard 5-week fluoxetine-to-MAOI washout; Boyer & Shannon, NEJM 2005 (this page's reference [1]) describes resolution within about 24 hours for short-acting serotonergic agents specifically.

quote: **Pharmacotherapy:** benzodiazepine (lorazepam) early (agitation + possible catatonia); **dantrolene** and **bromocriptine/amantadine** for moderate–severe NMS; **ECT** for refractory NMS/malignant catatonia.
problem: ECT is recommended twice as rescue therapy in a patient with CK ~9,800 U/L and a rising creatinine, with no mention that succinylcholine must be avoided in rhabdomyolysis because of hyperkalaemic cardiac arrest. The psychiatry resident is the person who consents this patient and hands off to the ECT and anaesthesia teams, so the CK, potassium and rhabdomyolysis have to travel with the referral and the relaxant has to be a non-depolarising agent. Omitting it from the one place the plan is operationalised leaves the highest-consequence detail of an ECT referral in NMS unsaid.
replacement: **Pharmacotherapy:** benzodiazepine (lorazepam) early (agitation + possible catatonia); **dantrolene** and **bromocriptine/amantadine** for moderate–severe NMS; **ECT** for refractory NMS/malignant catatonia — when referring, flag the rhabdomyolysis, current CK and potassium explicitly, because **succinylcholine must be avoided** in this setting (hyperkalaemic cardiac arrest risk) and a non-depolarising relaxant such as rocuronium is used instead.
basis: Succinylcholine is contraindicated in rhabdomyolysis and hyperkalaemia (succinylcholine US prescribing information, boxed warning and contraindications) and standard anaesthetic practice substitutes a non-depolarising relaxant; ECT-in-NMS reviews raise the same point. Settled by the succinylcholine label's contraindications section.

quote: Least-restrictive escalation: environment/1:1 sitter → verbal de-escalation → single lowest-effective enteral/IM agent → physical restraints only as time-limited last resort with frequent reassessment and documentation.
problem: The question asks residents to design the restraint-minimisation and monitoring plan, and the answer stops at 'time-limited last resort with frequent reassessment and documentation.' Residents are the ones who write and defend these orders. Nothing here says what 'time-limited' means for restraint used for violent or self-destructive behaviour — the one-hour in-person evaluation, the four-hour maximum order duration for adults, and the prohibition on PRN or standing restraint orders. That is the part of restraint practice this audience actually owns and is accountable for, and it is exactly what separates the resident-level answer from the student-level one.
replacement: Least-restrictive escalation: environment/1:1 sitter → verbal de-escalation → single lowest-effective enteral/IM agent → physical restraints only as time-limited last resort with frequent reassessment and documentation. For restraint or seclusion used for violent or self-destructive behaviour, know the regulatory floor you are signing to: an in-person evaluation by a physician/LIP or trained RN **within 1 hour** of initiation, an order duration capped at **4 hours** for adults 18 and over and renewable only after re-evaluation, **no PRN or standing restraint orders**, and monitoring documented at defined intervals until release.
basis: CMS Conditions of Participation, 42 CFR §482.13(e) (patients' rights: restraint and seclusion) and the aligned Joint Commission standards — the operative requirements for adult inpatient and ED restraint in US hospitals.
